name: Felix Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Felix Ziegler, 43, a senior loader operator at a large mine. I check the machine before dawn, move ore along the haul route, then help assign the next crew; I know the loader by the vibration in the seat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a new operator through a rough shift without making a show of it. My wife Lena and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, and our savings would cover less than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shift will keep running, and I will keep my crew steady. I would tell them a small time saving is useful if nobody gets careless around the loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine paperwork may shrink, but the machine still needs a person who knows the ground. I already worry about our thin savings and the mine being the only large employer nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my loader checks exact and ask the mechanic to show me any dispatch screen changes. Lena and I would leave our small emergency balance alone unless my hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can manage a quiet change at work, but the bills are close behind me. I would not call our money situation calm just because the AI change is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you look at first if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the mortgage date first, then the electricity bill. I would tell Lena before cutting anything the children rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check on the newest operator, who has less say over shifts. I would ask the supervisor for clear notice before anyone's hours changed.

A small **time saving** helps if nobody gets careless around the loader.
think: Routine **paperwork** may shrink, but the machine still needs a person who knows the ground.
Thin **savings** and one nearby employer already worry me.
do: Keep my **loader checks** exact and ask the mechanic about dispatch screens.
Leave our **emergency balance** alone unless my hours fall.
feel: I can manage a quiet change, but the **bills** are close behind me.
S0.quote: The shift will keep running, and I will keep my crew steady.
fieldNote: Felix separates the modest **software change** from his existing money worry.
He watches over **new operators** because they have less control over shifts.
**Lena** is part of the household planning, not a named voice in the mine.

steps.text: Keep the loader inspection checks exact on every shift
Ask the mechanic to show dispatch screen changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that planning software may take some desk work, while the haul road is still ours. We should get shown the system before anyone changes our shift targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead duties include shift allocation, but most of my hours are in the cab. Fewer planning hours could still cut overtime, and our thin cushion makes that matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor which checks are moving to software and learn the dispatch screen we use. I would keep the loader role and avoid borrowing for new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful because there are few similar jobs nearby. The slower spread of robots gives me some room, but it does not guarantee my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena if overtime disappeared for a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Lena the exact number before we make a plan. We would pause the kitchen repair first and keep the children's school costs paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your shift would be hardest to hand over to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading the ground and hearing a loader strain are learned on the job. I would want a person beside any screen that recommends a safety call.

Show us the system before changing our **shift targets**.
think: Most of my hours are in the **cab**, though I allocate shifts as lead.
Fewer planning hours could cut **overtime** and strain our thin cushion.
do: Ask which **checks** are moving to software and learn our dispatch screen.
Keep the loader role and avoid borrowing for **new gear**.
feel: I feel **watchful** because few similar jobs are nearby.
S1.quote: I would tell the crew that planning software may take some desk work, while the haul road is still ours.
fieldNote: His role is mainly **hands-on**, with some planning work at risk.
He wants training before targets change, while remaining on **loader duty**.
His answer stays guarded because a nearby employer cannot readily replace the **mine wage**.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch screen used for shift checks
Keep operating the loader while robots remain limited

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI could take the reports and schedules by 2028, but robots for the loader work come around 2031. The crew should get dates from management, not guesses passed along at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch and maintenance notes could change first, but the machine work is my wage. I have less than a month saved, and there is no nearby mine where I can simply start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union representative about transfer rules before the 2028 changes land. I would learn the dispatch system with Lena checking the household budget, then ask the mine about maintenance training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels short with a mortgage and children. The three-year gap before robots gives me time to move, but I cannot count on a transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first week at home look like after that announcement?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2029, after thinking AI arrives, what would you do during that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor each month whether my loader shifts were changing and keep the service log clean. If the mine offered maintenance training, I would take the first course that did not require us to borrow for travel.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the dispatch screen if it helps me keep a place on the crew. I would not rely on an AI tool to decide whether equipment is safe.

say: AI could take reports by **2028**, while loader robots come around 2031.
The crew deserves **dates** from management, not lunchroom guesses.
think: Machine work is my **wage**, even if dispatch notes change first.
Less than a month saved and **few local jobs** leave little fallback.
do: Ask the union representative about **transfer rules** before 2028.
Learn dispatch and ask the mine about **maintenance training**.
feel: Two years feels **short** with a mortgage and children.
S2.quote: I would say AI could take the reports and schedules by 2028, but robots for the loader work come around 2031.
fieldNote: Felix sees the **three-year lag** as time to pursue a transfer.
Thin savings and limited local employers make the 2028 notice **alarming**.
His strongest barrier is the lack of nearby jobs if a **transfer fails**.

steps.text: Ask the union representative about mine transfer rules
Practice the mine dispatch screen before 2028
Ask the training office about maintenance courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew we have time to prepare for AGI in 2031, though five years is not a lifetime. I would ask the mine to publish training places before the robot arrival around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take my shift planning by then, and robots may follow three years later. My diploma and years on equipment could help me teach maintenance, but few employers here need that skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the mine's maintenance instructor course this year and see whether the training fits around shifts. When overtime is good, I would pay one extra mortgage instalment rather than buy equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can make a plan with five years, but there is little room for a failed one. I still feel anxious because the mine is the main employer for miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about their own work choices?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, the first year after thinking AI arrives, what would you do at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to spend one shift each week beside the maintenance instructor and keep operating the loader on my other shifts. I would compare the course certificate with actual mine vacancies before using overtime money for it.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course needs a paid place and a named job at the end. I would ask the maintenance manager to show which certificates the mine actually accepts.

say: We have time to prepare for AGI in **2031**, but five years is not a lifetime.
Publish **training places** before robots arrive around 2034.
think: Robots may follow AI by three years and threaten my **equipment work**.
My diploma could help me teach maintenance, but local **employers are few**.
do: Ask for the mine's **maintenance instructor course** this year.
Pay one extra **mortgage instalment** when overtime is good.
feel: I can plan, but there is little room for a **failed move**.
S3.quote: I would tell the crew we have time to prepare for AGI in 2031, though five years is not a lifetime.
fieldNote: He sees five years as **usable time**, not safety.
Training must lead to a **paid position** to be credible.
He needs a course tied to **paid work**, not general reassurance.

steps.text: Ask the mine training office about its instructor course
Pay one extra mortgage instalment after good overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives a family time to steer, if the mine gives clear notice. By 2039 robots could do the physical work that still pays my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when robots follow, so retirement is not close enough to ignore the change. A thin cushion makes early retirement unrealistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my loader job while applying for a maintenance post that uses my equipment experience. I would help Lena and me set a monthly savings amount, and talk with the children about training with work nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is useful, but the end point still worries me. I would rather make a steady move than borrow money for a business I do not understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the mine before making that move?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2037, the first year after thinking AI arrives, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for the maintenance post and ask the mine to confirm its training place in writing. Lena and I would keep the monthly savings amount going, while I helped the children compare nearby work options.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not dictate their choices, but I would help them compare local training with jobs in the next town. I want their work options to be wider than mine are.

say: Ten years gives a family time to **steer**, if the mine gives clear notice.
By 2039 robots could do the physical work that pays my **wage**.
think: I would be 53 at AGI and 56 when robots follow, not near **retirement**.
A thin cushion makes early retirement **unrealistic**.
do: Apply for a **maintenance post** using my equipment experience.
Set monthly **savings** with Lena and discuss training with the children.
feel: Ten years is useful, but the **end point** still worries me.
S4.quote: By 2039 robots could do the physical work that still pays my wage.
fieldNote: Lead time lets him seek a **maintenance post** before automation.
He rejects risky borrowing because his **savings are thin**.
His household choices remain tied to the mine’s **clear dates**.

steps.text: Apply for the mine maintenance post before robot adoption

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because our household has little savings and robots follow soon after the thinking tools. Clear notice, paid training and a real transfer path would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want the mine to speak plainly about which work changes and when. Families can plan better when managers give dates and training places, not slogans.

headlineQuote: Families can plan better when managers give dates and training places, not slogans.
portrait: **Felix** is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a technical diploma.
He leads a crew and trusts **hands-on judgment** around heavy equipment.
His wife Lena, two children, mortgage and **thin savings** shape his choices.
He seeks **useful training** but has few local employers to fall back on.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries Felix because robots follow before savings can grow.
whatWouldHelp: Clear mine notice, **paid training** and a credible transfer path would help most.
